newsitem.title: USA: UK phone official urges US to end investment curbs.
newsitem.headline: UK phone official urges US to end investment curbs.

text.p: Britain's chief telecommunications regulator urged the United States to end restrictions on foreign ownership of domestic phone companies.
"The issue of ownership of telcos need not be and should not be an issue anywhere in the world," said Don Cruickshank, director general of Britain's Office of Telecommunications, or OFTEL.
He said in a speech to the Center for Strategic and International Studies that "anyone" can invest in the British telecoms market.
"You need to have a business plan and to apply for a license, but there are no competition authority hurdles to be jumped," Cruickshank said.
By contrast, he added, the United States has "detailed procedures necessary ...for taking any significant share in a U.S. telecoms company."
The Federal Communications Commission and the Justice Department currently are combing over the proposed merger of MCI Communications Corp and British Telecommunications Plc.

Regulators must determine whether Britain has opened its telecommunications markets to U.S. carriers before approving the deal. Lawyers expect, however, that U.S. regulators will sign off on the planned $20 billion transaction.

On other matters, Cruickshank warned against linking policies to ensure universal phone service with the financing of social policies -- such as hooking up schools to the Internet, as proposed in the United States.

Last November, state and federal regulators in this country proposed to set aside $2.3 billion a year to link schools and libraries to the Internet at discounted rates. The program would be paid for from revenues of phone companies, cable-TV operators and other communications providers.
Cruickshank said that telecommunications carriers already want to link schools to the Information Superhighway and that government policy is not necessary to spur them to do so.
"We feel we have cracked the problem of universal service and there are no social cost burdens on U.K. consumers," he said.
